'''Pierre Gabriel''' (1 August 1933<ref name="homepage">{{cite web |title=Biographie Pierre/Peter Gabriel |url=https://www.pierre-peter-gabriel-mathematics.ch/biography/ |access-date=21 December 2020}}</ref> – 24 November 2015), also known as '''Peter Gabriel''', was a French mathematician who worked as a professor at the [[University of Strasbourg]] (1962–1970), [[University of Bonn]] (1970–1974) and [[University of Zürich]] (1974–1998). He was an [[algebra]]ist with fundamental contributions to [[homological algebra]], the theory of [[Abelian category|abelian categories]], [[algebraic group]]s and the [[representation theory]] of [[Associative algebra|algebras]].

== Life and work ==
Gabriel was born in the French town of [[Bitche]] in [[Lorraine]], near the German border, a region that historically had been contested between France and Germany. Gabriel was bilingual and variantly used the first names ''Pierre'' and ''Peter'' in his publications. Throughout his life, he would forcefully argue for bilingualism and was active in several organizations supporting this goal.<ref name=":0" />

From 1953 to 1957 he studied mathematics at the prestigious [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École normale supérieure Paris]] and afterwards became a research fellow at [[French National Centre for Scientific Research|CNRS]] from 1957 to 1960. Mathematically, he was heavily influenced by [[Henri Cartan]], [[Alexander Grothendieck|Alexandre Grothendieck]] and [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], who all worked in Paris at the time.

His doctoral thesis, written at the [[Sorbonne University|Sorbonne]] under the direction of Serre, was defended in 1960<ref name="homepage" /> and published in 1962.<ref>Gabriel, Pierre, ''[http://www.numdam.org/article/BSMF_1962__90__323_0.pdf Des categories abeliennes]'', Bull. Soc. Math. France '''90''' (1962), 323-448.</ref> It contained important work about [[Abelian category|abelian categories]], a concept introduced by [[David Buchsbaum|Buchsbaum]] and popularized by Grothendieck a few years earlier. In his thesis, Gabriel studied the proper concept of [[Serre quotient|localization of abelian categories]], known as the Serre quotient or Gabriel quotient. With Michel Zisman he later proposed a more generally applicable concept of localization of categories and applied it to [[homotopy theory]], thereby axiomatizing simplicial homotopy theory.<ref>{{cite book
  | last1=Gabriel | first1=Pierre
  | last2=Zisman | first2=Michel
  | title=Calculus of fractions and homotopy theory
  | url=https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/GZ.pdf| publisher=Springer-Verlag| location= New York
  | year=1967
  | page=12
  | series=[[Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete]], Band 35}}
</ref> The thesis also contains an early "reconstruction theorem" allowing (under certain assumptions) to reconstruct a [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''X'' from the abelian category of [[quasi-coherent sheaves]] on ''X,'' by considering the spectrum of [[Indecomposable module|indecomposable]] [[injective object]]s in the category. This theorem, later vastly generalized by [[Alexander L. Rosenberg]] and now known as the [[Gabriel-Rosenberg reconstruction theorem]], forms a starting point for [[Noncommutative algebraic geometry|non-commutative algebraic geometry]].

In the early 1960s, Grothendieck and Gabriel collaborated in compiling the volumes [[Séminaire de Géométrie Algébrique du Bois Marie|SGA]] 1 and SGA 3. In particular, they established the [[Grothendieck construction]].

Gabriel collaborated with [[Nicolae Popescu]] in the study of abelian categories. In 1964 they published the [[Gabriel–Popescu theorem|Gabriel-Popescu theorem]], showing that every [[Grothendieck category]] is a Serre quotient of the category of all (right) modules over some (not necessarily commutative) unital ring.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Gabriel | first1=Pierre | last2=Popesco | first2=Nicolae | title=Caractérisation des catégories abéliennes avec générateurs et limites inductives exactes | mr=0166241  | year=1964 | journal=[[Les Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences]] | volume=258 | pages=4188–4190}}</ref>

With [[Michel Demazure]] he published a volume on [[algebraic group]]s in 1970, emphasizing homological methods and algebraic geometry in the style of Grothendieck. An English translation of the first two chapters of the book appeared in 1980.<ref>Pierre Gabriel, Michel Demazure: ''Groupes algébriques, vol. 1'', Masson, Paris, 1970. English translation of chapters 1 and 2: ''Introduction to Algebraic Geometry and Algebraic groups'', North Holland, 1980</ref>

In 1972 Gabriel published a fundamental result in representation theory, now known as [[Gabriel's theorem]]. He gives a complete list of those [[Quiver (mathematics)|quivers]] that admit (up to isomorphism) only finitely many indecomposable linear representations over a given field and furthermore describes those representations. His proof uses [[root systems]] and the [[Weyl group]].

Another important result in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, a collaborative effort of Gabriel, [[Andrei Roiter]], [[Raymundo Bautista]] and Leonardo Salmerón, appeared in 1985. Extending an earlier result by Gabriel's former doctoral student [[Klaus Bongartz]], it established the existence of multiplicative bases for algebras of finite representation type (i.e. those associative algebras over a field admitting only finitely many isomorphism types of indecomposable modules).<ref>{{citation|author1=Bautista, R.|author2=Gabriel, P.|author3=Roiter, A. V.|author4=Salmerón, L.|year=1985|title=Representation-finite algebras and multiplicative bases.|journal=Inventiones mathematicae|volume=81|issue=2|pages=217–285}}</ref>

Having relocated to Switzerland in 1974, he served as the president of the [[Swiss Mathematical Society]] in 1980–1981.

Gabriel and Bongartz wrote about [[covering space]]s in representation theory in 1982, building on earlier work by Gabriel's former doctoral student [[Christine Riedtmann]]. This led to effective algorithms for algebras of finite representation type.<ref>{{citation|last1=Gabriel|first1=Pierre|last2=Bongartz|first2=Klaus|title=Covering spaces in representation-theory|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|issue=65|year=1982|pages=331–378}}</ref>

Gabriel, his former doctoral student [[Bernhard Keller]] and A. V. Roiter published a book on the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras in 1997.<ref>Gabriel, B. Keller, A. V. Roiter: ''Representations of finite dimensional algebras'', Springer Verlag 1997</ref>

== Awards and recognition ==
He was awarded the [[Prix Francoeur]] in 1972. In 1986 he was a [[Plenary speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians|plenary speaker]] at the  [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] 1986 in Berkeley, explaining his work in finite-dimensional representation theory. He was elected a correspondent member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in November 1986.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://www.republicain-lorrain.fr/edition-de-sarreguemines-bitche/2015/11/29/deces-de-pierre-gabriel-militant-du-bilinguisme|title=Edition de Sarreguemines Bitche - Décès de Pierre Gabriel militant du bilinguisme|work=republicain-lorrain.fr}}</ref>
